scenario.title: One result, four reports, no signal for weeks
scenario.intro: A wheat project in South Asia measures adoption of early sowing among registered farmers. The same adoption result must reach CGIAR's PRMS, two investors with different templates and a national partner's own system. Meanwhile the field teams work in hill districts where there is no connection for weeks at a time. The team's first instinct is four spreadsheets and a lot of re-typing. This module shows how one validated record can travel to every destination without being collected twice.

objectives.text: Name the four layers of the Evidence Stack (direct observations, earth observation and sensors, external and context data, operational records) and state what each adds.
Trace one observation from Capture through Quality Assurance, Integration, Analysis and Use & Visualization, naming what it picks up at each step.
Explain the nine required functionalities and the design principles of the MEAL data system, including what the Data Group owns and what MEAL owns.
Apply collect data once: decide what changes when a new reporting template arrives and state what the KPI engine reports with each institutional result.
Apply the triangulation rule to judge whether a source strengthens a claim and when satellite or secondary data may not replace required ground measurement.

beats.hook: A project report says 3,000 farmers adopted early sowing. The framework does not treat that report as the unit of evidence. So what does it treat as evidence, and where does it come from?

example.title: Sort ten sources into the four layers
example.prompt: Drop each source into its Evidence Stack layer. Ask what it adds: the closest view of the state or change, spatial coverage, context, or traceability of delivery.

bins.label: Direct observations
bins.hint: Plot, farm, household, participant, trial, institution or result-object records.

cards.label: Crop-cut weights from 240 sampled wheat plots
cards.why: A plot record is the closest evidence of the actual yield. It permits disaggregation and re-analysis.

cards.label: Household survey records of which variety each farmer planted
cards.why: Farmer records used to measure adoption are the direct-observation example in section 2.6.

cards.label: Multi-environment trial results for a candidate line
cards.why: Trial records are listed with plot and household records as direct observations.

cards.label: Satellite imagery of crop cover across three districts
cards.why: Imagery adds spatial coverage, frequency and extrapolation between observed locations.

cards.label: Automatic weather station readings at the trial sites
cards.why: Weather and sensor data belong to the earth observation and sensors layer.

cards.label: National wheat production statistics from the statistics bureau
cards.why: Government statistics give benchmarks and denominators for interpreting change.

cards.label: Monthly grain price series from the market board
cards.why: Price and market series are context data, used as covariates when interpreting outcomes.

cards.label: Training attendance log with farmer identifiers
cards.why: Training logs trace who received a service, which later links delivery to uptake.

cards.label: Seed distribution records from a partner company
cards.why: Distribution systems and partner records are operational records, whoever holds them.

cards.label: The project's financial records
cards.why: Financial records are named in the operational records row. They show traceability from intervention to output.

bullets: The Evidence Stack has four layers: direct observations, earth observation and sensors, external and context data, and operational records.
Direct observations sit closest to the state or change being measured and allow disaggregation and re-analysis.
Not every indicator needs every source. The KPI reference sheet sets what is valid.

beats.hook: One enumerator weighs one crop cut on one plot. Eighteen months later that number is part of an institutional yield figure in PRMS. What happened to it on the way?

example.title: From a crop cut in a hill district to a PRMS entry
body: Capture. An enumerator in a hill district records the net-plot weight of a wheat crop cut on a tablet with no signal. The form was built from the yield KPI reference sheet, so it already asks for moisture, plot size and the plot's persistent identifier, which links back to the registered farmer. The record waits on the device until the team reaches a connection.

Quality Assurance. On sync, validation checks the weight against the expected range, confirms that the plot identifier exists and has not been submitted twice this season, and attaches a quality flag and a provenance entry: who collected it, when, on which form version.

Integration. The plot identifier connects the crop cut to the farmer's training record (operational records), to the district's rainfall series (external and context data) and to the satellite field boundary (earth observation and sensors). The data dictionary makes sure that yield means the same thing here as in every other project's records.

Analysis. At the annual KPI run, the KPI engine recomputes the institutional yield figure from all eligible plot records with the approved method and reports coverage, uncertainty and the method version. Nobody adds the project's reported yield into a total.

Use & Visualization. The same validated record feeds the project dashboard, the PRMS submission through the central mapping and two investor exports. When the quarterly review decides to extend early sowing to a fourth district, the decision log links back to the evidence that prompted it.

bullets: An observation passes through Capture, Quality Assurance, Integration, Analysis and Use & Visualization, in that order.
On the way it picks up a persistent identifier, quality flags, provenance and links to the other evidence layers.
Institutional figures are recomputed from the underlying records, which stay in the system so results can be recalculated and audited.

lessons.title: Satellite, context and operational data: what each adds

beats.hook: A satellite map covers every field in the district. A government series covers the whole country. The distribution log covers every seed pack. None of them is the measurement. Each adds something the others cannot.

example.title: Three sources, one adoption claim
body: The wheat project claims that 38% of registered farmers sowed early in the 2027 season. The claim rests on farmer-level plot records, the direct observations. Then three other sources arrive.

A satellite crop-calendar map shows sowing dates across all three districts, not just the sampled plots. Under the triangulation rule it can be calibrated against the plot records and used to upscale the estimate or to stratify next season's sample. It cannot replace the plot records, because the KPI method requires farmer-level measurement.

The national statistics bureau publishes total wheat area by district. That is a denominator and a benchmark: it tells the team what share of the district's wheat the registered farmers represent. It says nothing about who sowed early.

The partner's seed distribution log shows which registered farmers received early-maturing seed and when. Linked by persistent identifier to the plot records, it lets the team ask whether the farmers who received seed were the ones who changed their sowing date. That is the link from delivery to uptake.

Each source faces the same test: same construct, same population, same geography, same period, compatible definitions. A clear image from the 2025 season fails on period. A national series on total area fails on construct. Both can still give context. Neither strengthens the claim.

bullets: Earth observation and sensors add spatial coverage, frequency and extrapolation between observed locations.
External and context data add denominators, benchmarks and covariates. Operational records add traceability from delivery to later uptake.

A source strengthens a claim only when it matches construct, population, geography and period. Satellite and secondary data calibrate, contextualise, stratify or upscale; they do not replace required ground measurement.

beats.hook: Breeding data live in the breeding system. The budget lives in the finance system. The enumerators have no signal for three weeks. Does the MEAL data system copy everything, or connect to it?

example.title: Filling in the data architecture for the wheat project
body: The minimum package asks every project to name its authoritative systems, persistent identifiers, integration points, access rules, consent requirements and planned data flows. Here is how the wheat project fills that in.

Authoritative systems. Trial yields for the candidate varieties already sit in the breeding system, and the budget sits in the corporate finance system. The MEAL data system connects to both through integration rather than copying their records by hand. Farmer registrations and plot observations have no other home, so the MEAL data system holds them.

Capture. The field forms are built from the KPI reference sheets and run offline on tablets, syncing when enumerators reach a town. A low-bandwidth channel lets partner extension agents report sowing dates by message.

Configuration. The project does not build its own tool. It configures what it needs from shared, modular components: the farmer registry, the yield form, the validation rules for the sowing-date KPI. Open standards and FAIR principles mean the records can be found and reused by the next project in the region.

Ownership. The Data Group owns the infrastructure. The MEAL team owns the content: the indicators, the data dictionary and the quality rules. When the project wants a new validation rule, it asks MEAL. When sync fails, it asks the Data Group.

bullets: Where another system is the authoritative source for an indicator, the MEAL data system connects to it instead of copying data by hand.

The nine functionalities describe what the system must do, not a product: multi-channel capture, persistent identifiers, quality assurance and provenance, privacy consent and access, integration, KPI engine, analytics and geospatial, dashboards and reporting, learning and feedback.
Open standards, FAIR principles, offline operation and modular configuration. The Data Group owns the infrastructure; MEAL owns the content.

lessons.title: Collect once, report many times: investor reporting mappings and the KPI engine

beats.hook: The second investor's template just arrived. It wants the adoption result in a different layout, a different age band and a different season label. Your field team is still offline in the hills. What changes?

example.title: A new reporting template arrives. What happens, in what order?
example.prompt: A second investor sends a new adoption template for a result the project already collects. Arrange the steps the collect-once approach follows.

items.label: Compare the template's required fields with the source variables already collected
items.detail: The MEAL team starts from what exists, not from a blank form.

items.label: Add or update the central mapping from source variables to the template's fields
items.detail: Done by the MEAL team, centrally. A new system means a new mapping.

items.label: Set up the connection: a direct automated link where the system allows it, otherwise an export in the required format
items.detail: Two options, both fed from the same place.

items.label: Generate the submission from the same validated records used for institutional KPIs
items.detail: No result is entered a second time.

items.label: Confirm with the project that its forms are unchanged and nothing needs re-collecting
items.detail: Projects keep collecting through the same forms.

example.why: Section 4.3 says that adding a new reporting system, or adjusting to changed requirements, means adding or updating a mapping, not creating a new data collection. The MEAL team maps required fields to source variables, sets up a link or an export, and generates every submission from the same validated records. The field team never sees the template.

bullets: For each reporting system the MEAL team maps the required fields to source variables already collected, then sets up a direct link or an export.
Every submission is generated from the same validated records used for institutional KPIs. A new template means a new mapping, not a new collection.
The KPI engine calculates institutional KPIs from eligible records with the approved method and reports coverage, uncertainty and method version.

frames.narration: One crop cut. One record. Follow it through the five evidence functions and watch what it picks up.

Capture. The question comes first: what is the yield on this plot? The form is built from the KPI reference sheet. It records the net-plot weight, the moisture and the plot's persistent identifier. No signal, so it waits on the tablet.
Quality Assurance. On sync the record is checked for completeness, range and duplicates. It gets a quality flag and a provenance entry: who, when, which form version. From now on it can be audited.

The triangulation rule is a four-part match: construct, population, geography, period. An image from another season tries to count as support and bounces back. Context, yes. Triangulation, no.
